title: Release Airlock
pitch: The agent investigates. You retain production authority.
about_excerpt: The agent investigates. You retain production authority. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT in its in-app browser resolved the incident on the live URL: checkout restored, 2 of 2 approved by you, 0 writes went round you The plan opens onto why the order matters, a read opens onto the exact bytes the agent got, and every lever states its cost on hover Mid-incident: the service strip shows where the failure enters the chain, and the dock says how to attach an agent and what to ask What this page lets the agent do in Triage: 13 tools now, 14 more as the response stage moves on The command palette: every lever on the console, with what it costs At a glance. A deploy console where an agent reaches 27 WebMCP tools and cannot execute any of them; every write is a proposal a person decides on the same page, beside the evidence. Stage-gated surface (13 tools in Triage, 27 in Recovery), a plan tool for order-dependent fixes, provenance grading for writes justified by untrusted content, a live storefront that breaks and recovers. Verified: 229 unit tests, 144 hit-tested Playwright gates, 91 machine-checked scenario variants, Chrome webmcp-evals 24/24 live, Lighthouse agentic 4/4, 488 real-model runs. Found and filed against the spec: a host that both calls tools and drives the DOM can complete the page's human step itself (webmachinelearning/webmcp#288, with a one-file repro and a page-side mitigation verified against the host). Live: https://release-airlock.vercel.app · Repo: https://github.com/Sidharth1999/webmcp-airlock Inspiration An on-call engineer, mid-incident, probably awakened at like 4am by their PagerDuty, wants an agent's speed without handing it authority over production -- speed literally means less revenue lost to the business and less users impacted by outages. But we can't be careless about what agents are allowed to do with our systems. This is not a hypothetical based on some research. In the last fourteen months there have been nine documented cases of a coding agent destroying data, most of them with a permission system switched on that the agent talked its way past. Examples: https://adversa.ai/blog/ai-coding-agent-incidents/ https://mondoo.com/blog/5-lessons-from-9-seconds-ai-agent-deleted-production-database Every one of those permission systems lived either inside the model, which can be argued out of anything, or in a generic host confirmation, which knows the verb and the target and nothing about where the idea came from or what the operator is looking at. Three more facts shaped the design. The cost of an incident is deciding, not clicking ( Rootly ). Mitigation happens in a console, and the kill switch beats the rollback ( LaunchDarkly ). Stage-gated access is an established pattern, just-in-time and break-glass ( IBM ). And Chrome's own WebMCP security guide asks for exactly this shape: "it's impossible to guarantee safety inside of a large language model" ( secure tools ). WebMCP puts the tool server in the page. For this problem, that location is the whole point. The page is where the operator, the evidence, and the levers already are, so the page can be the authority on what the agent may do. What it does Release Airlock is a deploy and incident console where an agent can reach every lever, and not one of them moves without you. Live: https://release-airlock.vercel.app (opens inside a running incident; works in ChatGPT's in-app browser and in Chrome with WebMCP enabled) Source, MIT: https://github.com/Sidharth1999/webmcp-airlock Video: https://youtu.be/gqN-fXtGodk It exposes 27 WebMCP tools on document.modelContext: six reads, a notebook the agent writes its findings into, nineteen propose_* writes, and propose_plan. A write tool's entire effect is to put a card in front of the operator. The world moves when a person decides, and not before. The tool surface is a function of console state. Move the response stage from Triage to Diagnosis to Recovery and tools are registered and unregistered underneath the live session (AbortController, so a real host fires toolchange). Triage grants 13 tools. Nothing that touches production exists in Triage; it is absent, not gated. A withdrawn tool leaves a tombstone, and explain_surface tells the agent why its capabilities changed. The gate is re-checked when the human decides, against the stage the operator has set by then. The page grades the evidence it served. Every read is audited into the same event log the page renders from. When an agent proposes rolling back a deploy id that appeared nowhere in the console's state and reached the agent only inside a customer-supplied log line, the card quotes the line, names the read that served it, and promotes the write to a two-key approval. For the operator, an incident is a stitching problem. The hard incidents are the ones where the order you do things in decides the outcome, and no single screen says "shed load first." The agent is good at exactly that stitching, and the console lets you audit the stitching before you let it act: One ledger. Every beat is a row on one spine: connect, each tool call, each finding, the plan, each step, what that step did. A tool call opens onto the exact bytes the agent got back, with the log position they reflect and a link to the console surface they came from. A citation is a place. "Contention cleared (#42)" is a button that lands you on log line 42. The agent objects before your click. Reach for a control it has ruled out and its reasoning appears beside that control. It counsels; it never blocks. A plan numbers the console rows it will touch and prices every step. Every executed write says what it did. When nothing moved, it says why: "No effect: scale to 9 has no effect, the autoscaler ceiling for api is 6." The customer is on screen. A storefront breaks when the incident starts, shows the status post you approved at step 4 word for word, and takes payments again when the fix lands. The receipt reads 7 of 7 approved by you, 0 writes went round you. While an agent host is attached, approval is a held gesture, not a click. The console stands on its own without an agent. Every lever is clickable by hand, states its cost, and is worth having on a bad day. How we built it One event log is the truth. The world is a pure fold over it; the UI, the tool results, and the metrics all derive from (events, world). There is no second source of state to drift. A Web Worker owns the log ; the main thread renders and forwards. The tests and the unattended driver invoke tools through the same execute path real WebMCP uses. 27 tools, documented from the registration path itself. The surface reference in the repo is generated by walking the real registration code through every stage, so it cannot disagree with the bundle. Reads return pages under 1.2 KB with a log position on every answer. Writes return only a proposal id. The gate is checked on both sides. video_transcript_excerpt: Hi, my name is Sid. I'm here to showcase how Web MCP allows agents to identify issues and propose fixes during incident ops management, all while a human retains full authority of the system. So, what are we looking at over here? We've got the incident console of a system managing an online storefront, and unfortunately, we are dealing with an incident at checkout. So, first thing I'm going to do is acknowledge the incident, mark it sev one, and in the background, I've actually kicked off an agent that's going to start investigating the issue with the system, and hopefully eventually propose a fix. Its work will eventually show up on this right-hand panel, um and this panel has three different modes. Each mode gives the agent a different set of capabilities. Triage mode is all about just understanding the state of the system, whereas uh recovery mode gives it the tools needed to actually fix the issue. As you can see, the agent has already started calling tools. One tool it just called was to update the status of the system on the the live site, which you can see showed up over here. Now, it's also started calling tools that help it understand the state of the system. Think like deploys, logs, recent changes, and eventually, it should be able to correlate all of this information to understand like what's going on with the system, and hopefully eventually propose a fix as well. So, let's let it do its thing. Um you can see like what the agent is also thinking uh over here on the ChatGPT UI as it's calling these tools. So, you're always in the loop, you know, understanding what's going on, um as the agent is like reasoning through the state of the system. Um eventually once it's identified the root cause, it should show up here. Um it found out that there was a bad deploy that wasn't enforcing retry logic the right way and overloading the systems. So, eventually it's going to propose the tools that actually allow it to bring the system back into health. So, the first thing to do is cap checkout and then finally roll forward to the fixed deploy and you can see the system is back in health and what we're left with is a clean ledger of every action the agent performed and all of the evidence it gathered to bring the system back to health and finally a flat line of errors. So, great news. Um so yeah, that's Airlock. Thank you guys for watching.
